36-025.r: DDT (dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane) → non-biodegradable pollutant; insecticide that is fat-soluble, stores in body fat and gets more concentrated up the food chain.

36-026.r: Herbicide → butachlor (acetanilide class), used as granules in rice farming.

36-027.r: Carbon-14 (radiocarbon dating) → age of fossils, wood, bones and shells (time since death); based on C-14 decay, half-life about 5,730 years.

36-030.r: Radioactive dating → measures the (absolute) age of rocks and other geological features.

36-031.r: Age of the Earth → uranium (uranium-lead) dating; Clair Cameron Patterson used it for one of the earliest accurate estimates.
36-031.t: Carbon dating → fossils; uranium dating → age of the Earth.

36-032.r: One carbon credit → right to emit one metric ton (1,000 kg) of CO2 or an equivalent greenhouse gas; idea came from the Kyoto Protocol, 1997.

36-033.r: Direct Air Capture (DAC) → removes CO2 from ambient air for storage underground (sequestration) or products: plastics, food industry, synthetic aviation fuel with hydrogen → all three correct.

36-034.r: BRIT (Board of Radiation and Isotope Technology) → isotope technology unit of the Department of Atomic Energy; HQ at Vashi, Navi Mumbai.

36-035.r: Philosopher's wool (lana philosophica) → zinc oxide (ZnO): alchemists burnt zinc in air and got white woolly tufts; used in paints, zinc ointment, sunscreens.

36-036.r: Pungent smell near urinals → ammonia; urine is about 91-96% water, with urea about 2.6%.

36-037.r: Antihelium-4 (heaviest antimatter, Brookhaven, 2011) → helps probe antimatter stars and galaxies and understand the universe's evolution; not mineral or oil prospecting → 2 and 3.

36-038.r: Cirrus cloud thinning and sulphate aerosol injection into the stratosphere → geo-engineering ideas to reduce global warming (sulphate aerosols reflect sunlight).

36-039.r: Cloud seeding for artificial rain (also to cut air pollution) → silver iodide (main) and potassium iodide (auxiliary); dry ice or sodium chloride also used.

36-040.r: Artificial clouds/rain → silver iodide particles sprayed on clouds from aeroplanes; sometimes dry ice (solid CO2) or sodium chloride.

36-043.r: Amount of rain → depends on humidity (moisture) in the atmosphere.

36-044.r: Blue vitriol → fungicide; eosin → red ink; silver iodide → artificial rain; zinc phosphide → rodenticide.

36-045.r: Correct pair: zinc phosphide → rat poison. Fixes: silver iodide → artificial rain; silver chloride → horn silver; zinc oxide → philosopher's wool.

36-046.r: Kevlar → synthetic fibre; taxol → anticancer drug; zinc phosphide → rodenticide; nitrocellulose → explosive.

36-047.r: Wrong pair: silver bromide – artificial photosynthesis → silver bromide is used in photography. Correct: silver iodide – artificial rain; lithium bicarbonate – rheumatism; milk of magnesia – antacid.

36-048.r: Silicon carbide → artificial diamond; carbon fibre → aircraft; carbon dioxide → photosynthesis; dichlorodifluoromethane → refrigerator.

36-049.r: Iron → haemoglobin; lead → storage battery (lead-acid); silver (bromide) → photography; copper → lightning conductor.

36-050.r: Morphine → analgesic (opioid from opium); sodium → kept in kerosene oil (very reactive); boric acid → antiseptic; German silver → alloy (copper, nickel, zinc).

36-051.r: Skin cancer → ultraviolet light; noise pollution → decibel; global warming → carbon dioxide; ozone hole → chlorofluorocarbons.

36-052.r: 'Metal of the future' → titanium: light, strong, corrosion-resistant; used in aerospace, buildings, sports goods and surgical implants.

36-053.r: Wrong pair: silver – electric bulb → tungsten is used in bulbs. Correct: magnesium – fireworks; uranium – atom bomb; zinc – galvanization.
36-053.t: Silver is the best conductor and reflector, but bulb filaments are tungsten.

36-054.r: Vermillion → mercuric sulphide, mercury(II) sulphide (HgS); brilliant red pigment first made from the mineral cinnabar; insoluble in water.

36-056.r: Dry washing (dry-cleaning) solvents → petrol, benzene and alcohol all used (also camphene, kerosene) → all the above.

36-057.r: Red ink → eosin (tetrabromofluorescein), a red dye; most red inks are its dilute solution.

36-058.r: Sodium chromate (Na2CrO4) is yellow; with no yellow option the book picks red (options: blue, red, green, black).
36-058.c: Sodium chromate is actually yellow; yellow is not among the options, so the book picks red.

36-059.r: Crimson red in crackers → strontium salts. Barium → green; magnesium → bright white; calcium → orange; copper → blue; sodium → yellow/gold.

36-060.r: Acetone → nail polish remover; carbon tetrachloride → fire extinguisher; hydrogen peroxide → dressing wounds; liquid ammonia → refrigerant.

36-061.r: Wrong pair: hydrochloric acid – accumulator cell → the lead-acid accumulator uses sulfuric acid. Correct: potassium chlorate – matchbox; manganese dioxide – dry cell; uranium – atom bomb.

36-062.r: Main element in matchboxes → phosphorus (striking surface); it reacts with potassium chlorate on the match head to ignite.

36-063.r: Safety matches → red phosphorus (with phosphorus trisulfide); match head: potassium chlorate, red lead, antimony sulphide, glue.
36-063.t: Red phosphorus for safety matches; white phosphorus is the one that glows in air.

36-064.r: Glows by itself in air and darkness → white phosphorus, a waxy transparent solid giving a greenish-white glow (phosphorescent).

36-065.r: Carbon nanotubes (CNTs) → Sumio Iijima, Japanese physicist, often cited as their inventor.

36-066.r: Desalination plants → Lakshadweep and Chennai (book accepts both); India's first at Kavaratti, Lakshadweep (2005): LTTD plant, 1 lakh litres a day, by NIOT.

36-068.r: Reclaiming alkaline soil → calcium sulphate (gypsum, CaSO4·2H2O); its calcium replaces sodium in the soil.

36-069.r: Edaphic → relating to soil (drainage, texture, chemical properties such as pH).

36-070.r: Cryogenics → study and use of materials at very low temperature; e.g. liquid hydrogen (fuel) and liquid oxygen (oxidizer) in rockets.

36-071.r: Chemical weapon of the First World War → mustard gas (sulfur mustard, dichlorodiethyl sulphide); poisonous, causes skin ulcers.

36-072.r: Mustard gas (sulfur mustard) → chemical warfare agent first used effectively in World War I by the German army near Ypres, Belgium, in 1915.

36-074.r: 'Mustard gas' → actually a liquid at room temperature; harms skin, eyes and lungs; symptoms appear after 1–6 hours.

36-075.r: Smoke screens (to hide military operations) → fine particles of titanium oxide (titanium dioxide) dispersed in air; zinc chloride also used.

36-076.r: Agent Orange → herbicide and defoliant containing dioxin, used by the US military in the Vietnam War (Operation Ranch Hand, 1962-1971); causes cancers, birth defects.

36-078.r: Incorrect: nucleus breaking apart is 'fusion' → that is fission; fusion joins nuclei into a heavier one. Correct: Darwin – evolution; dry ice = solid CO2; Graham Bell – telephone.

36-079.r: Dry cell (zinc-carbon or Leclanché cell) electrolytes → ammonium chloride and zinc chloride; no free liquid, so it works in any position.

36-082.r: A true: a dry cell cannot be recharged. R false: its chemical reaction cannot be reversed. Dry cell: zinc pot with manganese dioxide, sal ammoniac, carbon.

36-083.r: Dry cell (primary cell) → stores chemical energy, which it changes into electrical energy.

36-084.r: Car battery electrolyte → sulfuric acid (H2SO4), a strong acid.

36-088.r: Rechargeable batteries of torches, shavers → nickel and cadmium electrodes (nickel hydroxide cathode, cadmium anode); potassium hydroxide electrolyte.

36-089.r: Microwave oven → magnetron tube, a high-powered vacuum tube producing microwaves from electrons in combined electric and magnetic fields.

36-090.r: Freon → refrigerant; tetraethyl lead → anti-knocking agent; benzene hexachloride → insecticide; carbon tetrachloride → fire extinguisher.
